new_statements.quote: In Nimaḍi a phonological-word is having only one heavy stress /´/ and other syllables in the word are having secondary or weak stress /`/. At word-level stress is not phonemic as it is in English. But if somebody is not putting a proper stress on a proper syllable, it looks unnatural to a native speaker [...] (p.90) Since stress is not phonemic at syllabic-level no fixed rules can be made. Some general observations about stress are given. [...] (ii) When a word is dis-syllabic having one short and another long vowel and if the long vowel is not preceeded by a consonant cluster; the syllable having long vowel has a heavy stress :- /jəm-í/ 'freezed (f.)', /jəmín/ 'land', /cúrəṇ/ 'powder' [...] (iv) If in a word both the vowels are short and the second syllable is closed the first syllable has a heavy-stress. /gə́rəm/ 'hot'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word has exactly one heavy (primary) stress, whose position is non-contrastive but predictable from vowel length and syllable shape: a long vowel attracts the stress (jəmín, kanún, vərdát, Ityádi; but a short first vowel wins if the long vowel follows a cluster: cə́mpi); with two long open syllables the first is stressed (níḷi), with several long vowels in a trisyllable the second (jaúga); with only short vowels, a closed final syllable puts stress on the first syllable (gə́rəm, ə́Urət, ə́gəhən) while an open final syllable takes the stress itself (jəgə́, cəhəkəṇə́). Only utterance-level 'extra heavy' emphatic stress is phonemic.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Other syllables carry secondary or weak stress (left unmarked); in derived and compound words 'generally the first stress is heavy followed by a secondary stress' (ə́pə̀c 'indigestion', mái bàp 'protector'), p. 92.
new_statements.exceptions: Author frames the rules as 'general observations' rather than fixed rules; long vowel preceded by a consonant cluster loses stress to a preceding short vowel (cə́mpi 'massage'); emphatic extra-heavy stress shifts freely by focus (p. 89). Phonetic correlates: tenseness, vowel lengthening, consonant gemination, raised pitch, reduced length/aspiration in unstressed syllables (pp. 92-93).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word in citation form; description is of Central ('standard') Nimadi, Khargone-Khandwa, from two rural informants plus c. 3000 words / 1000 sentences (ch. 1, p. 8). Hans 1960 (Hindi, p. 121) gives a cruder and partly conflicting account (disyllables usually initial, trisyllables usually medial).
new_statements.identity_note: Lekhwani 1979 explicitly describes Central Nimadi (Khargone to Khandwa), which he calls the standard variety, and lists Eastern (Harsud, Bundeli-influenced), Northern (Malvi-influenced), Western (Bhili-influenced) and Southern (Khandeshi-influenced) sub-dialects as differing; all fall under Glottolog nima1243 / ISO noe (no sub-dialect glottocodes). Hans 1960 is a Nagpur University thesis on Nimadi generally. Glottolog's retired 'Bhalay' (bhal1245) speakers use Nimadi.

sources.note: One heavy stress per phonological word; word-level stress not phonemic (only utterance-level 'extra heavy' emphatic stress is contrastive); position given by 13 'general observations' driven by vowel length and syllable closure: a long vowel attracts stress (jəmín 'land', kanún 'law', Ityádi), two long open syllables -> first (níḷi), two short vowels with closed final -> first (gə́rəm), two short open -> second (jəgə́), trisyllables all-short closed-final -> first (ə́Urət), all-short open-final -> last (cəhəkəṇə́); compounds: heavy then secondary.

sources.note: Impressionistic: Nimadi tends to stress 'a'; 'in disyllabic words stress is usually seen on the first syllable (sandūk, kutto, paisā, biḍā, aundho); in trisyllabic words stress is usually found on the middle syllable (kaṛhvo, kabūlī)'; sentence stress falls on the first syllable of the first word of each breath-group; emphatic stress changes meaning. Older, philological, partly at odds with Lekhwani's length-based rules.
